newsitem.title: CHINA: China says Hong Kong frames policies in 1997.
newsitem.headline: China says Hong Kong frames policies in 1997.

text.p: China signalled on Tuesday it was keeping a close eye on the return of Hong Kong this year, especially when Beijing's decision-makers set the course of economic policy.

The People's Bank of China, the central bank, said it would maintain "appropriately tight" money supply because of a crucial Communist party congress late in the year and the return of the British colony on July 1.

"In 1997 the key financial requirements are... to seriously apply the appropriately tight monetary policies to keep the rise in prices for the year below last year's (6.1 percent) level," the Financial News said.
The newspaper, published by the central bank, said these objectives were needed this year "...ahead of the 15th party congress and the recovery of the exercise of sovereignty over Hong Kong".
It did not explain why such purely political issues were being used to set financial goals.

China has said this year would be one of the most significant of the communist era with the return of Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, ending 150 years of British rule, and the party congress, which will set policies for the next five years.
Chinese economists have said Beijing would proceed cautiously on economic and financial reform this year, fearing it could ill afford setbacks before these two political milestones.
Western diplomats said the central bank's statement highlighted the political nature of economic and financial decisions in China.
They noted that competing interests within the ruling Communist Party, both at the national and regional levels, were pushing for central government support for their own projects.
Money supply would affect the funds available to finance development or keep ailing state enterprises operating, they said.
"Money supply has always been linked to special interest groups," said a Western diplomat who monitors China's economy.
Diplomats also said, however, that the central bank could be using the party's two main political concerns to pursue its own policy objectives.
Economic policies were more likely to be adopted if they appeared to aid a smooth transfer of power in Hong Kong and did not disrupt the party's political objectives at the congress.

Chinese Vice Minister of Foreign Trade An Min said on Monday it would support Hong Kong's efforts to expand foreign trade relations after the territory returns to Beijing's control, provided such ties did not undermine China's sovereignty.
State media said Hong Kong businessmen would retain preferential tax status for investments on the Chinese mainland.
China gives foreign investors lower tax rates than Chinese companies and treats businessmen from Hong Kong as foreigners.

Foreign businessmen, however, are made to pay a whole range of fees that are not required from local businessmen. They also must hire employees through special government agencies, boosting their operating costs.
